claim: Many authors start with the figures when writing a scientific paper.
source: Many authors start with the figures when writing a scientific paper, but it is easier to tell a good story if you start with the Introduction and the Results, and leave the figures to later.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about common practice among scientific authors.

claim: It is easier to tell a good story if you start with the Introduction and the Results, and leave the figures to later.
source: Many authors start with the figures when writing a scientific paper, but it is easier to tell a good story if you start with the Introduction and the Results, and leave the figures to later.
evidence: This is the author's opinion based on experience with scientific writing.

claim: In operas, the libretto is usually written before the score.
source: Take operas for example: even though they are all about the music, the libretto is usually written before the score.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about opera composition practice.

claim: It has become common practice to prepare figures before writing the text in scientific papers.
source: That said, I do understand why it has become common practice to prepare figures before writing the text.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about current scientific writing practices.

claim: It is easier and more fun to make figures than to think or write.
source: It is easier and more fun to make figures than to think or write.
evidence: This is the author's opinion about the relative difficulty of different writing tasks.

claim: Making figures before writing text is a displacement activity.
source: But all this is a displacement activity (definition: an unnecessary activity that you do because you are trying to delay doing a more difficult or unpleasant activity).
evidence: This is the author's characterization of the practice, with a definition provided.

claim: You need to know what data you have and don't have before you write.
source: This is not to say that you should ignore your data at this stage: you absolutely need to know what you have and don't have before you write.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for scientific writing.

claim: PowerPoint slides work well as a digital bulletin board for collecting rough versions of panels.
source: A simple expedient is to collect rough versions of panels with minimal editing on a digital bulletin board – PowerPoint slides work well.
evidence: This is a practical recommendation based on the author's experience.

claim: In the author's lab, people often bring excellent figures along with fragments of text or no text at all.
source: In my lab, and despite my pleas, people often bring me excellent figures along with fragments of text or no text at all.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the author's personal experience.

claim: As drafts progress, panels are often added, removed, altered, and always rearranged.
source: As we go through draft after draft, panels are often added, removed or altered – and always rearranged.
evidence: This is based on the author's repeated observations in their lab.

claim: The 'figure first' strategy is a product of Photoshop and Illustrator.
source: The 'figure first' strategy is a product of Photoshop and Illustrator.
evidence: This is the author's inference about the historical development of scientific writing practices.

claim: In the past, micrographs were generated with an enlarger and graphs with Letraset.
source: Back in the day, when micrographs were generated with an enlarger and graphs with Letraset, it was necessary to have a definitive plan before starting to print and draw.
evidence: This is a historical fact about past scientific practices.

claim: Old methods of figure preparation required having a definitive plan before starting to print and draw.
source: Back in the day, when micrographs were generated with an enlarger and graphs with Letraset, it was necessary to have a definitive plan before starting to print and draw.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the technical limitations of older methods.

claim: Old methods of figure preparation helped make sure that thought preceded action.
source: I have no nostalgia for those cumbersome methods – but they did help make sure that thought preceded action.
evidence: This is the author's inference about the benefits of older methods.

claim: More often than not, the data don't provide an answer to the precise question you began with.
source: At some point, you feel that you have gained enough insight to begin writing a paper – but more often than not, the data don't provide an answer to the precise question you began with.
evidence: This is stated as a common occurrence in scientific research based on experience.

claim: If you try to fit the answer to the question, you risk ending up with a compendium of results that is less cohesive than it could be.
source: If you try to fit the answer to the question, you risk ending up with a compendium of results that is less cohesive than it could be.
evidence: This is the author's inference about the consequences of a particular writing approach.

claim: Starting with the answer and figuring out what the question should have been is counterintuitive but works.
source: Instead, start with the answer, figure out what the question should have been, and build on that. This seems counterintuitive, but it works.
evidence: This is the author's recommendation based on experience.

claim: You don't need to present experiments in the sequence in which they were done or explain why they were actually done.
source: Think hard about the best order in which to present them, feeling free to take advantage of what is, to my knowledge, the only fiction that is fully allowable in a scientific paper: you don't need to present experiments in the sequence in which they were done or explain why they were actually done.
evidence: This is stated as an allowable practice in scientific writing.

claim: A scientific paper is not an autobiography; the story you tell should be about the science, not about you.
source: Put another way, a scientific paper is not an autobiography; the story you tell should be about the science, not about you.
evidence: This is stated as a principle of scientific writing.

claim: The order of presentation can be, and often should be, quite different from the order of execution.
source: The order of presentation can be, and often should be, quite different from the order of execution.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for scientific writing.

claim: In presenting your results, you have to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.
source: In presenting your results, you have to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.
evidence: This is stated as an ethical requirement for scientific writing.

claim: You don't have to tell the whole truth in presenting your results.
source: What you don't have to do is tell the whole truth.
evidence: This is stated as an allowable practice in scientific writing, with the caveat that selection is permitted.

claim: If you have results that call your conclusions into question, you need to present them and explain why your conclusions are still justified.
source: There is one crucial caveat: if you have results that call your conclusions into question, you need to present them, and explain why your (possibly modified) conclusions are still justified.
evidence: This is stated as an ethical requirement for scientific writing.

claim: You don't need to describe everything you did in a scientific paper.
source: My point is that you don't need to describe everything you did.
evidence: This is stated as a principle of scientific writing.

claim: Blaise Pascal wrote an aphorism generally credited to Mark Twain: 'I would have written a shorter letter but I didn't have the time.'
source: This is difficult, as noted long ago by Blaise Pascal in an aphorism generally credited to Mark Twain: "I would have written a shorter letter but I didn't have the time."
evidence: This is stated as a historical attribution of a famous quote.

claim: The Discussion provides an opportunity to highlight what you want the reader to remember – the key results and principal conclusions.
source: Next comes the Discussion, which provides an opportunity for you to highlight what you want the reader to remember – the key results and principal conclusions.
evidence: This is stated as the purpose of the Discussion section.

claim: The Discussion is conventionally structured by summarizing results in a paragraph, following with sections devoted to major points, and finishing with a brief concluding paragraph.
source: This is conventionally done by summarizing the results in a paragraph, following with sections devoted to major points, and finishing with a brief concluding paragraph.
evidence: This is stated as a conventional format for scientific papers.

claim: You don't have to rehash all of the results in the Discussion.
source: To that end, remember that just as you don't have to include marginally relevant data in the Results section, you don't have to rehash all of the results in the Discussion.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for writing the Discussion section.

claim: The Discussion should have between two and five subsections.
source: Instead, plan a small number of subsections (between two and five) within the Discussion, in each of which you state a conclusion, summarize the results that support it, and relate it to previous work in the field.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for structuring the Discussion.

claim: Citing key papers acknowledges your debt to your predecessors and avoids being accused of claiming more novelty than is justifiable.
source: By citing key papers, you acknowledge your debt to your predecessors and avoid being accused of claiming more novelty than is justifiable.
evidence: This is stated as the purpose and benefit of citing previous work.

claim: Acknowledging weaknesses in your argument is not only honest but can be helpful: it is harder for a reviewer to be harshly critical if you have already been self-critical.
source: Acknowledging weaknesses in your argument is not only honest but can be helpful: it is harder for a reviewer to be harshly critical if you have already been self-critical.
evidence: This is stated as a strategic benefit of self-criticism in scientific writing.

claim: Be sparing in claiming that experiments to test your speculations are in progress, as the reviewer or editor might be tempted to ask you to resubmit once you've done these experiments.
source: Be sparing, though, in claiming that experiments to test your speculations are in progress, as the reviewer or editor might be temped to ask you to resubmit once you've done these experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a strategic warning based on potential reviewer/editor responses.

claim: In the author's lab, they have a practice called 'paper bashing' in which they devote a long lab meeting to going over a paper line by line.
source: In my lab, we have a practice called 'paper bashing' in which we devote a long lab meeting to going over a paper line by line.
evidence: This is a direct description of a practice in the author's lab.

claim: Almost every time a lab member or other reader points out a problem with a word, sentence, section or conclusion, they are right, and something needs to be done.
source: Here's the main lesson I have learned from this painful but invaluable process: almost every time a lab member or other reader points out a problem with a word, sentence, section or conclusion, they are right, and something needs to be done.
evidence: This is stated as a lesson learned from repeated experience with the 'paper bashing' process.

claim: The particular improvements that readers suggest are often not the best ones.
source: On the other hand, the particular improvements they suggest are often not the best ones.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the author's experience with feedback.

claim: The author is better than readers at coming up with useful solutions because they have thought about the work more deeply and are more familiar with the results and the literature.
source: You have thought about the work more deeply than they have, and are more familiar with the results and the literature, so you are probably better than they are at coming up with useful solutions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about why the author is better positioned to find solutions.
